stem:
An emergency doctor sees a man who has used GHB every two hours, including overnight, for several months. Four hours after his last dose he is increasingly tremulous, sweaty and tachycardic; during assessment he becomes confused and reports seeing insects. Glucose is normal, and the team is investigating other causes of delirium. He requests a few tablets to manage at home.

Which plan best addresses the immediate risk?

options.label: A
options.text: Start a standard fixed-dose oral diazepam regimen on a general medical ward
options.explanation: GHB withdrawal often needs much larger and more frequent benzodiazepine doses than alcohol withdrawal and can deteriorate within hours. A general ward regimen is unlikely to be enough.

options.label: B
options.text: Admit for monitored benzodiazepine titration with early critical-care review
options.explanation: Rapidly escalating withdrawal with early delirium after round-the-clock GHB use can become severe and benzodiazepine-resistant. It needs monitored, titrated benzodiazepine treatment with critical-care involvement.

options.label: C
options.text: Observe without medication until 24 hours after his last dose, then reassess
options.explanation: Withdrawal in round-the-clock users begins within hours of the last dose, and he is already delirious. Waiting delays treatment.

options.label: D
options.text: Give haloperidol for the hallucinations while further tests are awaited
options.explanation: Antipsychotics do not treat withdrawal and lower the seizure threshold. The hallucinations here are part of the withdrawal delirium.

options.label: E
options.text: Give a single diazepam dose now and review him on tomorrow’s ward round
options.explanation: A single dose and delayed review ignore how rapidly GHB withdrawal escalates. He needs continuous monitoring and titration.

context: GHB withdrawal can become severe within hours, particularly after frequent dosing throughout the day and night.
